utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. I'm Tom Hannis for the Prosecution, along with Gerry Dobbyn, Milena [sic] Vilova, and our Case Manager today is Indah Susanti. I meant to say Marina Vilova, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. May the witness be escorted back to the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Andan. I give you the usual reminder about your solemn declaration before Mr. Hannis continues. Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Andan, I was curious about one thing. At the beginning of the war when you eventually left Sarajevo and came over to the Serbian MUP side, you first told us you were in Ilidza for a while and then in Raca. As I understand it, most of your police career up to then, you had worked in the Sarajevo area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a correction. I did not go to the Serbian MUP side. I joined the MUP of Republika Srpska. All my pre-war career was in Sarajevo, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Given your experience and familiarity with the Sarajevo area, were you surprised that you were sent to Brcko rather than being given some assignment in the Sarajevo area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not surprised because I had placed myself at their disposal, and the assessment at that point in time was probably that I should help out where the security situation was the most complex. As a soldier and an officer, I accepted that and I went out to that assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did it ever pass through your mind that perhaps Mr. Stanisic didn't trust you in the Sarajevo area and wanted to send you somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I think that Mr. Stanisic didn't even have time to think of some Dragomir Andan. He had quite a few problems. He couldn't really be giving me any thought. I've already explained this at the very outset: I was given a task, and I went to Brcko. So I cannot say and I cannot have any suspicions of that kind, whether he sent me to Brcko, Mr. Stanisic, because of some lack of trust. Least of all did he have any reason to think about me because he had so many problems to deal with throughout Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's talk about Brcko again for a moment. You told us while you were there you did have some dealings with the army. Did you know a Captain Cuturic with the Eastern Bosnian Corps intelligence organ? Did you ever meet him or know him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how you understood this co-operation of mine or ours with the authorities in Brcko, but I did tell you that several times I had meetings with them. The first meeting took place at our request, and we asked for part of the police force to be returned from the front line. Then several times we talked about the security situation or we asked for certain favours, as it were. So there wasn't any kind of intensive co-operation underway, at least as far as I'm concerned. As for Mr. Cuturic, this is the first time I hear of that particular last name, if that is his last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we show the witness Exhibit P154. I think this is still an MFI exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, on the screen --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's tab number 251 in the Prosecution binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, on the screen, in a moment, you'll see this document; it's dated the 29th of September, 1992. And in a moment we'll see the last page where the editor is a Captain First Class Simeun Cuturic. I will tell you it's a -- it has a bit of a retrospective about events in Brcko, and in particular it's talking about events in the period of May through June at the facility called Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to the first page again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And he's describing briefly what happened after the bridges over the Sava River had been destroyed. He says the town was flooded by different "patriotic" orientated individuals who used "devotion to Serbism" as an excuse for robberies, rapes, and, as a result of that, murders for no justified reason. He mentions Mauzer and some of Arkan's Men. Is that consistent with the information you learned about what had happened in Brcko after the bridges were destroyed at the end of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, if you wish to hear my comprehensive opinion of this particular piece of information, I'd have to read out the whole report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In order to save time, what I'll do is perhaps give you the report at the end of this first session and ask you to work during the break again just to save us courtroom time. Thank you. I will then turn to Bijeljina. We talked a bit about Bijeljina before, and I want to ask you about the interview that I think you read yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think the Registry officer may have a hard copy of that. This is 65 ter 1967. It's our tab 308. If we could hand a hard copy just of the newspaper article. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, you told me yesterday you had a chance to read this during one of the break, and it's an interview, I think in 1994, with Predrag Jesuric, who you told us was at one time the chief of the CSB in Bijeljina. Did you get a chance to read it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again a correction, as far as the interpretation is concerned. It is "Jesuric" not "Jesovic." And I did have an opportunity reading this interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I need to defend the translators. Probably the problem you're having is that the interpreters are having a problem with my pronunciation of the name and that's why it's not coming across as you would expect it to. I'll try to do a better job. In the newspaper article, Mr. Jesuric talks about his relationship, his working relationship, with Mr. Savic, Mauzer, and at page 2, my English, he mentioned Savic as the untouchable commander of the planned and well-thought-out defence of the town, and says that all the participants were subordinated to him and the Crisis Staff that worked out of the SDS offices. Is that consistent with what you found in Bijeljina when you went there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot speak about the period before my arrival there, but it is obvious that when Mr. Davidovic and I arrived in Bijeljina, Mr. Mauzer behaved exactly this way, as has already been described here. I've already said that we had received instructions not to yield to any kind of political pressure, to carry out our work professionally. And that is how we came to Bijeljina. I'm primarily referring to Vukovic and myself. My impression was after a while and after the clashes that we had with Mr. Mauzer and after attending a meeting - now, was it the Crisis Staff of the municipality or some other body? - Mr. Davidovic and I were there anyway and Mr. Mauzer sat next to the chairman of that meeting and of course everybody who took part in the debate first addressed Mauzer and only then the chairman. So I understood what Mr. Mauzer's role was. I think that he had expected us as members of the Ministry of the Interior probably to come and report to him about our own work. In my view, that is where the basic conflict was between Mr. Mauzer on the one hand and on the other hand the police structures that were carrying out their work in a lawful manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your experience in Bijeljina, is it correct that the problems were not only paramilitaries from outside, from Serbia, but problems with the locals, in particular Mr. Savic, Mauzer, and his forces? Wasn't that one of the biggest problems for you in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I have to say something by way of a small clarification. Either during my direct examination or while I was being examined by you, I mentioned that there was this formation of Mr. Blagojevic's and we did have certain problems, individual problems, with members of the Serb Radical Party. At first they did not want to respect the curfew, and when they were drunk they would sometimes fire into the air. But we did call Mr. Blagojevic in for an interview. We drew his attention to the behaviour of his men. And I have to say that afterwards we didn't have any problems with Blagojevic. But we had an on-going conflict with Mauzer. And I know that the second time when he surrounded the police station in Bijeljina, I mean Mr. Mauzer, that Blagojevic's men wanted to make themselves available to the Ministry of the Interior. We did not allow that. We did not allow that. We said that we did not need any kind of help and that we would try to resolve that in a lawful manner. So there were problems with paramilitary formation in Brcko, but Mauzer was our major problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we've heard from you before and seen from the documents that this was being reported about. You were reporting up the chain about Mauzer and the problems he was causing, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We were reporting to the local authorities and the Ministry of the Interior. I don't know now whether in the information that was sent on to Mr. Karadzic the problem of Mauzer was mentioned too, but we did report about the problem with Mauzer. We did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But it appears that nothing was done about it. You didn't get any support or direction from political authorities or from higher-ups to do anything about Mr. Mauzer, did you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From a formal and legal point of view, if we are going to look at it that way, Mauzer was not supposed to have any kind of contact with the political structures. As a military formation, he was supposed to be under the command of the Eastern Bosnia Corps. And it was the commander and his associates that were supposed to have greater responsibility in this respect. We reported to them several times about what was going on. The commander knew when Mauzer brought tanks to the police station in Bijeljina. In these talks, they kept promising us that they would deal with the situation, that they would overcome these problems, and they just said, Don't go into any kind of conflict. Of course, we could not avoid doing our job. So I would have considered myself to be co-responsible if I had turned my head the other way when Mauzer's forces were doing what they were doing and if I said, Well, let them do whatever they were doing. We asked the commander to have that problem resolved because from a formal and legal point of view he was under the military. On the other hand, he had every political support in the Bijeljina municipality and from this interview that Mr. Jesuric gave to Drago Vukovic, I see that that's exactly the way it was. I've put the picture together. So we on the one hand have one order from the ministry or minister and that is implement the law, take care of public law and order, prosecute criminals, et cetera. On the other hand we have this armed force opposing all of that and we cannot deal with it, and we informed the Ministry of the Interior about that as well, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as I understand it, during your time in that area between mid-June and mid-August 1992, as far as you know Mauzer and his Panthers were never officially fully subordinated to the army; right? In spite of the fact that Colonel Ilic had promised on more than one occasion that they were going to do that, it never happened, as far as you know, during the time you were there; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you yesterday, one of our proposals was to have Mr. Mauzer's unit relocated from Obrijez, I think the name was, and to be transferred to the barracks. In that way they would be under the control of the military in some way, but that was not done. So I cannot talk about that period -- I can only talk about that period, rather. I cannot talk about what happened later. But that is what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask you a question about Cedo Kljajic. I believe it was between the time you first went to Brcko but before you went to Zvornik for the Yellow Wasp operation. Do you recall an incident when you and Mico Davidovic came across Mr. Kljajic doing something with the driver's licence forms in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Kljajic was filling out a traffic licence on a typewriter. That came as a surprise to us. And I think that Mico Davidovic reacted rather sharply. He can be quite rash. He said, What are you doing, Cedo? Have you gone that low to type out a traffic licence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what did Mr. Kljajic say in response to that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say anything. He was perplexed. He blushed, the two of us left. I think that I took Mico by the hand and took him out. And when we were in out in the hall, Mico said, Let me tell him, let me tell him. And I said, Mico, let's go; we have other things to do downstairs. And that's how it went.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You don't know about any further conversation in which Mr. Kljajic indicated that he needed to do something to supplement his income, and this had to do with stolen or confiscated Golf vehicles that were going to be taken to Serbia and sold?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This had nothing to do with a Golf. I heard about that later. And I think it was Mr. Davidovic who told me about that, that some soldier, whose last name was Ribin [phoen], I know full well, at some check-point a BMW was taken away from him and it ended up at the car market in Bubanj Potok near Belgrade. I was told that Mr. Kljajic's driver had taken the BMW there to that car market and sold it, used car market. Let me be quite clear. I did not document that in any way, but I was informed by Davidovic. That was his information, everything that had happened in Belgrade. I had no opportunity to check that out. Now, was that just after the Zvornik action? At any rate, it's that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let me show you another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is P -- I'm sorry, 1D97. I think it was the Defence tab 76 or Prosecution tab 146.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, this is a document you were shown before. It's actually a copy of the report you sent in about establishing law and order in the area of the Bijeljina CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is the one that had a handwritten note on it apparently from Radovan Karadzic to the effect of, Keep up the good work, or, Keep on enforcing the rule of law. When was the first time you ever saw that part that's apparently written by Mr. Karadzic? Did you see it in 1992? Did you only see it when you were interviewed in 2005 or when proofing for testifying here?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember when I saw this note made by Mr. Karadzic. It is possible that I saw it back in the analytical department of the Republika Srpska MUP and that I made a copy for myself. I don't know the exact date. It may have been before the interview with you or it may have been in 2004. I was a director at the time, and somebody from the analytical department told me about it. All the documents had already been taken to The Hague Tribunal and I think that that was when I took a copy of this document for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take it from that you did not see it at any time in 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I apart from writing those nice, encouraging words, do you personally know of anything that Mr. Karadzic did to support your efforts in Bijeljina? For example, did he call the Bijeljina local political leaders and encourage them to support what you were trying to do, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know whether he spoke to anyone on the basis of this memo of mine. I have no knowledge whether anybody from the municipal government structure spoke to Mr. Karadzic in regard to this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: His note's dated the 2nd of August, 1992, and about three weeks after this you had been suspended and removed from the MUP. Did Mr. Karadzic do anything like he apparently did nor Malko Koroman to try and keep you in your job? Apparently not; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he did not have any obligation to do anything like that. After all, he was the president of the republic and I was a member of the Ministry of the Interior. My problem should have been resolved at the level of the ministry. Mr. Karadzic also should not have interfered into the issue of the replacement of Malko Koroman in Pale. That's my own personal opinion. It's all something that had to be left within our house, so to speak. I don't know. If he went to speak to someone, he should have spoken to the prime minister or the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, I share your personal opinion about whether Mr. Karadzic should have interfered in the matter of the replacement of Mr. Koroman, but the fact is he did. And I suggest to you that one reason why he did for Mr. Koroman and he did not for you, one possible explanation is that what you were doing and what you had done was not popular with the top leadership in the Republika Srpska, whereas what Mr. Koroman had done wasn't a problem for them; would you agree that's possibility?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm just asking myself if Malko Koroman had been the commander of a police station in Rudo or in Gacko whether the reaction would have been same. Mr. Karadzic lived in Pale. There was a problem, an armed group had assembled around the police station. Pale is a small town and he definitely must have seen it, and that is maybe the reason why he reacted in the way that he reacted. If all this had happened in Gacko or in Kljuc or in some other place, I don't know whether he would have been informed about it at all. And then it would have been up to the organs of the Ministry of the Interior to resolve the situation. So with all due respect, please do not think that I'm defending anybody here, but I think that the place where it happened had something to do with the fact that Mr. Karadzic reacted. I was a little bit further away, and I assume that the flow of information was not as easy, but the fact is that things happened to me that, well, that happened to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the fact is, Mr. Koroman not only wasn't replaced, he eventually went on to become head inspector of the RS MUP, which I take it is a promotion and a pay raise; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you asked me yesterday about the salary. At the time, it was maybe two or three packs of cigarettes. That's not important. Now looking back with all the experience that I have, I think that they created a space within which Mr. Koroman could be removed from Pale, transferred to Bijeljina, and given a promotion. And I remember that when he was transferred to Bijeljina he didn't do any hard work there. It was all done in order to put another person there in order to calm down certain structure and political authorities. I think that it was a skillful manoeuvre that they managed to execute in order to avoid any further armed rebellions or pressures on the police station, and that was a way in which they had managed to resolve the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks for that. Next I want to show you a document related to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is Exhibit P337. It's tab 97 of the Prosecution list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, do you know where the municipality of Kalesija was? I hope I pronounced that correctly, K-a-l-e-s-i-j-a.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where is it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's about 20 or 30 kilometres away from Zvornik in the direction of Tuzla. 30, maybe 35. I think that that's the distance. Okay, let me say around 30 kilometres towards Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. This document is dated the 29th of June. It appears to come from Minister Mico Stanisic, although that signature looks more like I think what we've had evidence about as being from Mr. Njegus. It's directed from the minister to Zvornik Public Security Station saying it's necessary that Zvornik allow the Kalesija SJB to use a certain car. Was it -- was it normal for the minister to send something like this directly to a public security station rather than going through the CSB? Because most of the documents that we've seen emanating from the minister go first to the CSBs which then disseminate them out to the SJBs. Isn't that how it worked?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not the only example. There are other examples in which somebody else signed the document on behalf of Mr. Stanisic. I would call it a crisis of authority. The question is, if something like that is sent by the chief of the centre, is the chief of the station going to actually obey it. Well, somebody else signed this, but we have here the minister's name, so people are definitely going to think, Oh, we now have to obey the order coming straight from the minister. Of course, you're quite correct when you're wondering why would the minister resolve problems of Kalesija and vehicles in Kalesija, but I also know how things functioned down there. There are many people who would say, Oh, what is this person going do, what does this minster want to do? As I already stated, there was a crisis of authority, because people, especially those among soldiers who were the first to take up arms, would normally say What? Where was he back in April 1992 when I took up arms and started fighting? So I think that I have seen another similar document also requesting an allocation of another impounded vehicle in a similar manner. Of course, there was a practice that impounded vehicles could be temporarily used, and I can tell you that that was the practice after the war. You know, they would say, well, now we have this vehicle here and let it be temporarily used in the police until we get a permanent solution. Indeed for a while such vehicles would be given permanently to the police. I'm not quite sure how this is regulated by law and I don't know whether this happens in Western Europe, but, yes, there were cases in which these vehicles were given to us for permanent use. So I hope that my explanation is correct. I told you what I think. I think that this is an example of the crisis of authority. I will write it up and then there will be the minister's name. I think I can claim here under full responsibility that Mr. Stanisic was not even aware that this particular document had gone out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you personally have no way of knowing whether or not he may have discussed it with Mr. Njegus and given him authority to sign for him; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I cannot know that. But the man is here, he is alive. I assume that he is going to say something about this. But looking back, I have to say that I think that he probably did not know that this was signed for him. Maybe it was signed by somebody from his office or one of the chiefs of the operative departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who Radomir Njegus was and what position he held in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I know Radomir Njegus. I think that in 1992 he was assistant minister for personnel. I'm not sure what exact name of the administration was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on to another topic. I want to discuss with you a little bit about the Mico Stanisic's men or the Malovic unit. And you looked at a bundle of photographs yesterday. If we could have the usher hand those to you. This is from Exhibit 65 ter 20145 at tab 318 of the Prosecution's list. And I think you told us during the break you had gone through and put little red stickies for me on those whom you recognised as being members of Mr. Malovic's unit in 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was not entirely sure for one person whether I know him privately or whether he was a member of the unit at the time, but I marked everybody else. As far as I know, these are the persons that were with Malovic at the time in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if you could, I think the easiest way to do this, Mr. Andan, is if you will tell us one by one. I see the one on top you have a red sticky on. If you could give us the eight-digit number at the top of the page, I think it's at the top of the page above each of the photographs. If you could tell us that eight-digit number and the name of the person, that will go into the record and then we'll know which ones you've picked out for us.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, Predrag Bartula. And then there is a numerical number at the top: 06491588.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's just right. Can you continue with any others that you identified.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milenko Samardzija, numerical number 06491590. Nenad Markovic, numerical number 06491595. I'm not sure about this one. I told you that I wasn't sure about one of them, did I see him in the unit or privately in Sokolac. It's Milenko Ecimovic, numerical number 06491597. So maybe he was, maybe he wasn't. Darko Arbinja, 06491598. Zeljko Maricic, 06491610. Ognjen Neskovic, 06491619. Dragoslav Markovic, 06491622. And Slobodan Kezunovic, 06491626.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Andan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender this exhibit. I will tell you this has -- the entire document has more than just these photographs. It was in response to a request for records from the prosecutor's office in Bijeljina, which has this as part of their file related to the case involving the murder of the three Muslim families that we've talked about before. I don't need that other information, so perhaps what I can do is restructure the exhibit with just the photographs this witness has identified and then substitute that in e-court, if that's agreeable with the Court and with the Defence

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, definitely ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, could you explain to us what it is you want to show with this exhibit other than what we have by way of the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can link these names to names in payroll list for Dusko Malovic's units which are already in evidence, and then with that I have the link of a living witness who saw these people as has identified them as members so we don't have confuse about whether, Oh, well, that's somebody by the same name. And, you know, This Bartula is not the same one that's on the payroll list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps I can understand the motives of Mr. Hannis to offer this, but I definitely object that the whole document would be admitted. Because what was shown to the witness were the photographs of the persons and their names, whatever is the information contained in this documents, and he recognised that. The rest, not a single question was asked about the rest of the document, and there's some documentation for 2008 and so on and so forth. And therefore I do object that the whole document is admitted. However, Your Honours, we are not disputing the fact that these persons which are in the actual transcript are or were according to the witness members of this unit from Sokolac. We are not disputing that. We never -- honestly, we never intended to dispute these facts, because we think they are completely relevant, but that's another story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, I just want to be sure that I understand you. In terms of the document, your objection is that it -- the whole document not be admitted, or that if it comes in that the whole document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry I wasn't clear. I object that the whole document be admitted. However, I do not object and I do not contest the fact that these photographs are from these persons and these photographs which the ERN numbers which the witness read can be admitted in evidence if Mr. Hannis insists after this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis, following on from the question that Judge Harhoff asked and having regard to Mr. Zecevic's concession, the -- whereas it is -- I suppose I could understand your wanting to make sure that the photographs remove any suggestion that would be made that the names, notwithstanding the similarity of names of different individuals, having regard to what Mr. Zecevic has said, is it necessary to go through this complication of -- to go through an exercise which we now know would be a somewhat complicated one?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, in terms of the exercise, that's the exercise I think the Prosecution has to do in restructuring the exhibit, and that's not too complicated. We're happy to do that. The saying is, a picture's worth a thousand words. This is not going to add greatly to the burden on the Trial Court in terms of exhibits you have to deal with. And I can see there's still a possibility there may be some occasion with a future witness where it may be useful or helpful to have a photograph of one of these individuals to show them and address some question with them. I think it's not too much to ask. I think it's relevant. And I would again urge that you receive this document in the modified form that we propose to make to address Mr. Zecevic's concerns about material other than these photographs and the personal data for the persons pictured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the decision of the Chamber is by majority, Judge Harhoff dissenting, that the -- pending the modification which has been offered by Mr. Hannis, that the six photographs would be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2346, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. We'll make that change and then notify Defence counsel or run it by them before we make the request to substitute it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, the last one we looked at is still on the screen, I think. That's Slobodan Kezunovic. He was the deputy directly under Mr. Malovic in this unit, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you another exhibit related to the Malovic unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 3560 at tab 262. [Microphone not activated] I've got a hard copy if the usher would assist. I'll hand it to you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I've got a hard copy I would like to hand you with the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is a report dated the 13th of October, 1992. If you go to the last page, you see it comes from a senior investigator named Goran Saric. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's the Goran Saric that was the commander of the Special Forces of the Republika Srpska MUP, then I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. He is reporting about some events that happened in the area of Milici on or about the 1st of October, and he mentions the Special Unit Malovic being in the area of Vlasenica on the 29th -- or, I'm sorry, around the 29th or 30th of September, 1992. I'm looking at page 2 of the English. I'm not sure where it is in the B/C/S, but it's the paragraph that talks about "on October 3rd a problem arose when special commander Boban did not want to get engaged without Malovic." Do you find that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take it Boban in this context is probably Slobodan Kezunovic, would you agree, because as the assistant commander, he would be the one in charge when Malovic wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe it calls for speculation, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I think he's in a position to make a comment and then Your Honours can decide how much weight to give it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot be certain that the man in question is Slobodan Kezunovic. But based on this sentence, this is a possible assumption. I cannot confirm that however. If the full name were in the document, then I could confirm. But this is a nickname, so maybe it's him, maybe it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You know Boban is a nickname for Slobodan; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You know Mr. Zecevic, Slobodan Zecevic, here, he goes by the nickname of Boban; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll accept that as a stipulation without requiring the witness to be put under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Anyway, Mr. Cvijetic is Slobodan but they call him Slobo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, my point is, Mr. Andan, that Boban is a common nickname for persons named Slobodan; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, having regard to the witness's answer earlier, you've taken this as far as you can, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if the witness could take his headphones off, I'll make a comment. Mr. Andan, could you remove your headphones. Thank you. Your Honours, this was a small unit. Slobodan Kezunovic has been identified as the deputy. I'll double check, I'm not sure there are any other Slobans [sic] in the unit, and so therefore I would argue that there is at least some logic to my position. There's also a reference further on in this document to Boban and his unit, indicating it was a Boban who was in position of authority within the Malovic unit and I'll leave it at that. The witness can put his headphones back on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Andan, on Friday you were asked a question about your experience with the Malovic unit when they were in the area in July -- June, July, August of 1992 and providing some assistance to you during certain operations. You said, at page 21463: "They went about their job very professionally. Whether anything happened later, I don't know." But since that time, since 1992, you did have occasion to hear allegations that the Malovic unit had been involved allegedly in the murders of three Muslim families in the municipality of Bijeljina; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll have to correct the first part of your sentence. They did not provide assistance to us. They placed themselves at our disposal and took part in all operations with us. It is correct that I said that they acted very professionally while we were working together, and it's also correct that I said that one of the options discussed concerning the murders of the Sarajlic family, as far as I remember, involved Mr. Malovic's name, whether himself or with his unit. But one of the options or one of the assumptions, rather, was that Mr. Malovic with his unit was involved in the murder of that family.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to show you Exhibit 65 ter 20141. This is tab 316 in the Prosecution's list. And again I can hand you a hard copy. Do you recognise this document? It's dated the 12th of December, 2007. It's an Official Note apparently of a conversation you had with the Prosecutor's Office in the special department for war crimes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I must say that the first allegation or the first sentence in this Official Note is false. I remember the event and I don't deny talking to the representatives of the OTP in Sarajevo, but I did not enter the facilities of the BH Prosecutor's Office voluntarily. I requested Mr. Jurcevic [phoen], the state prosecutor of BH, to receive me, and as I have said, he did, and I offered him to go into detention voluntarily due to the state I was in pursuant to the information sent out by Carla del Ponte that I was part of an organised crime network and that I was supporting Radovan Karadzic. I've described that already. And at the end of the conversation, Mr. Jurcevic said that my problem was not with the state Prosecutor's Office of BH but rather with the OHR. He asked me if I was willing to go and talk to Ms. Bozidarka, I didn't remember her name but I know that it was a woman, and I accepted. And the conversation took place, that is correct. And another remark with regard to the text. I told to this person Bozidarka that one of the stories that had reached me, and it was the most widespread, that Dusko Malovic or his unit took part in that killing. That is the truth. So number one, I didn't go there voluntarily; and secondly, I said that one of the versions or, rather, the most common story was that involving Mr. Malovic. I accept the rest of the text, but I had to make these corrections. With all due respect for Bozidarka, if she wanted to have a story involving me, then as a professional she should have taken my statement which would have been asked --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: -- which I would have signed --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- at the end of that interview. I hope that you agree with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I see at the end the name is Bozidarka Dodik. Does that refresh your memory as to her last name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means nothing to him [as interpreted]. I was beside myself at the time. I only remember that it was a woman. I didn't care about the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Have you seen this written Official Note before today?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you want to take a few minutes to read it, because I'm sort of relying on what's said here as being what you actually said at the time. So I need to ask you if you can confirm that, and I certainly want to give you an opportunity to review it if you think you need to. I see you finished reading. Do you have any comment? Please tell me.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did finish. I have another correction maybe. It is correct that the chief prosecutor summoned me, but I didn't come voluntarily, I went to see him for another matter. And I stand by what I have just said, that one of the assumptions but the one that was most popular was the version involving Mr. Malovic's unit. If I had had any specific knowledge, I would have found a way to convey it to the authorities in charge. I don't know what stage the investigation of the state prosecutor's office is in, but I did say that one of the versions, the one that was being mentioned most frequently, was the one involving Mr. Malovic's unit. There was also a press release by the radicals by which they denied all that, and that's also what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But Ms. Bozidarka --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Wait a second, I see Mr. Zecevic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, the last part of the answer was not recorded properly. Perhaps witness can repeat his answer, because it is recorded as: "There was also a press release by the radicals by which they denied all that, and that is also what I said." That is not what he said and then that's not what he said just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, you heard what Mr. Zecevic just said. It's my understanding, from part of the case file, that there was a press release by the radicals, by Mirko Blagojevic, at the time saying that Malovic's men were responsible for these murders. Is that what you were saying? What was the last part of your answer about the press release by the radicals?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was misinterpreted and that you also misunderstood what I said at the end. I said that I stand by the last paragraph of this Official Note, which says that the representatives of the Serb Radical Party issued a press release over SIM Radio, which was a broadcast that the Sarajlic family had been killed and that it was denied by Mr. Tomislav Kovac. This last paragraph, I said that the radicals conveyed that information and that it was denied by Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you say last paragraph, you're talking about the last paragraph on page 1 of your B/C/S version; correct? Because that's the paragraph -- it's not the last paragraph in the entire Official Note, but it's the last paragraph on that first page; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. It's the last on the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what I -- I understand your position about saying you didn't go voluntarily or on your own initiative as described here, but did anyone coerce or did anyone torture you or make you some promise, give you some reward for giving this statement? Bozidarka didn't mistreat you to get you to give your statement, did she?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course she did not. I told you that Mr. Jurcevic asked me after the interview if I was willing to go to the war crimes department to talk to an investigator about something. He didn't really say exactly what I was supposed to speak about. And I said, No problems, and I went to Bozidarka's office. But I may be wrong in this, but this sounds -- sounded to me like that I came from Banja Luka and they wanted to interrogate me about some circumstances or that I was there to give a statement about some circumstances, both of which is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. A couple of questions. In the - one, two, three - fourth paragraph on the first page, you're quoted or noted as having said that: "In July 1992 the unit came from Sarajevo to Bijeljina at the order of the then minister of the MUP of the RS Mico Stanisic, and that they wore grey/white camouflage uniforms which is why they were called Djetlici." "Woodpeckers" in English. Do you remember yesterday I was asking you about nicknames and I asked you if you heard the term "snowflakes" being used in connection with this unit. Now here you're reported as referring to them as woodpeckers. Is that a nickname you heard used for Malovic's unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that mostly they were called Malovic's men or Mico's men. You said that they were called snowflakes and I said woodpeckers. Now, I'm really not sure what they were called, nor do I care much, but I know that the unit existed, it was commanded by Malovic whose deputy was Kezunovic, and these are undisputed facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One more question before the break. At the bottom of English page 1, and for you I think it's near the top of page 2, says that you explained: "According to the MUP's organisation at the time, Dusko Malovic's special unit was directly subordinate to Cedo Kljajic." Is that correct, in September of 1992 at the time of the murders? Is that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if we understand each other properly, but as soon as she left Pale, she was re-subordinated -- or rather, it was re-subordinated to the highest-ranking officer and that was Cedo Kljajic, and it was given at the disposal of Davidovic and me. He was the highest ranking at the time and, of course, the unit was re-subordinated to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender 65 ter 20141.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we object. I believe the Trial Chamber gave a ruling on the fresh evidence and just last week or this week, I'm not sure anymore, maybe on Monday. So the Office of the Prosecutor needs to fulfill a number of requirements in accordance with the jurisprudence before they can be allowed to have this document or these kind of documents admitted during the Defence case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Do you have reply, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this -- I'm not sure when we received it. Looking at the ERN 0649, that's a pretty high number, and that means it's a fairly recently received document. I think it was -- I'm not sure when we got it or when it was disclosed, but we didn't know it was something we were going to use until we became aware that Mr. Andan was going to be called as a witness. So it was not something -- by the Defence. So it was not something we could have used earlier. I think it's relevant. It's going to be important to you in deciding on the evidence this witness has given. It will bear some weight on decisions about what he says today to the extent that it may be different than what he said in 2007. And, therefore, I think it's also relevant and necessary for Your Honours in making final determinations in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, we will consider the issues and give our decision when we return. So we take the adjournment now, to come back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, have you reached a decision on my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, continuing where we left off at the break, could -- inasmuch as this is your application, Mr. Hannis, can you assist by telling us what this document is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And apart from that, when the Defence would have learned about it, when it would have been disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think the Defence, as far as getting it from us, only got it when Mr. Andan took the stand to testify, because it was a new document that we added on our list of documents to use with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And when was it added?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before he started to testify. It was in our original list at tab 312, which we filed the minute he started to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And the first part of the question, in summary, what is the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This is something we received from the prosecutor's office in Bosnia. I think it's part of a file. It's related to Exhibit P1543, which is already in evidence, which is from the prosecutor's office in Bijeljina. The investigation involving the murder of the three Muslim families. So it's related to that case file. And as you can see, we say it's important and relevant for you because it goes to a number of contested issues in the case. The position of the Malovic unit, under whose authority were they, and this is a disputed issue. The Prosecution's taken the position that they were directly subordinated to Mr. Stanisic. The Defence has said otherwise. We have some evidence to that effect. This witness has said that when they arrived they were temporarily subordinated to him and Mr. Davidovic. In this statement in 2007 he says they were directly subordinate to Mr. Kljajic. So it goes to that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Andan, could you take your headphones off, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And there are parts of it, too, that I would argue should be before you in terms of judging his credibility, because I think some of what he says here is contradicted by other documents already in the case or to be in before I finish with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You said something -- before you -- in terms of judging his credibility, is that the primary purpose of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, it's not the primary purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] We have some questions for Mr. Zecevic. I just wanted to know if there's anything else you want to add, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Not at this time. I was just going to argue some of the law to you. We filed a motion yesterday concerning some of the documents for Mr. Bjelosevic where we set out the applicable law, and I think the Judges are familiar with that, but if you want to have a convenient place to look at it, that's in our filing from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic, this is a document which, if I might summarise Mr. Hannis's position, as I understand it, that was disclosed to the -- well, was notified to the Defence as soon as they learned that this witness was testifying. Could you expand on your -- the basis of your objection to its admissibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, the document was not disclosed to us at the moment when the Office of the Prosecutor was aware of the -- of Mr. Andan testifying in this case for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. What I was saying was they were notified when he took the stand and began testifying. Not when we got their 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: When -- Mr. Hannis, when did the Office of the Prosecution got this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] We received this document in 2009.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: In 2009. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I think May of 2009.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, that's number one. The number two, again, brings us back to our request made to the Office of the Prosecutor on -- based on Rule 66(B), where we requested all the documents pertaining to all our witnesses. The third thing is, if this document was a part of the file which is already in the -- as Mr. Hannis said, it is connected, because the part of the exhibits is the file which was received probably in 2009 and which was compiled by the Office of the Prosecutor in Sarajevo in 2009 concerning the murder of Sarajlic family in Bijeljina. Now, the whole file, what Office of the Prosecutor thought or relied on, is already an exhibit in the case. Now, this document was a part of the file. It was taken out because it's an Official Note created by the Prosecutor. It's not signed by the witness. So, therefore, that goes to the -- to the position of the Office of the Prosecutor concerning the Official Notes that we discussed some time ago, if Your Honours can recollect about the contents of the official notes. What my -- if my recollection is correct, the Official Note was admitted on the purpose that -- that not for the truth of its content, but for the fact that the Official Note was taken. Because the Office of the Prosecutor was against the admittance of such documents because they say there might have been, for whatever reasons, not accurate description of what the person said. Now, if that standard apply for Official Notes, then it should apply for this Official Note as well, because it's not signed by the witness. In any case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I might just hold you at that point, Mr. Zecevic. If - and I underline if - it is being offered merely for the fact of its existence, as contrast to the truth of its contents, what prejudice is there to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There is no prejudice to the Defence if it's offered for the pure existence of this document. It is not disputed at all. But what -- if it -- if this would be a document which the Office of the Prosecutor offers concerning the credibility of the witness and not for the truth of its contents, we wouldn't object. But Mr. Hannis said its primary goal is to admit this document for the alleged truth of its contents. And we say, Your Honours, the Office of the Prosecutor had this document in their possession. If they thought it was a document which could further their case, they would have offered it when they offered the whole case file received from the Office of the Prosecutor in 2009. And it has been admitted, despite our objection. We objected to that document being admitted because we say it's irrelevant for the issues of this case because this incident is not in the indictment. But nonetheless we stay on the position that at this point in time and in this -- during the Defence case the Office of the Prosecutor should not be allowed, according to the jurisprudence, existing jurisprudence of this Tribunal, should not be allowed to enter this fresh evidence because they cannot fulfill the requirements set by the jurisprudence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, we didn't have the chance to read the document in entirety. What would be the prejudice to the Defence if it comes in for the truth of the contents? I'm referring to what the Appeal Chamber decision is learning us as how we should deal with this, if there is prejudice and if that prejudice can be remedied.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the prejudice would be that, Your Honours, since this document was drafted by somebody else, it might not contain the actual wording of what the witness said during --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But he's accepted the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he accepted the contents. But I'm not sure if that means that he is accepting all the way how it was put on the document, you see, Your Honours, because it's a bit different than what his testimony is, and that is going be the prejudice for the Defence. In my opinion. Otherwise the Office of the Prosecutor would not be insisting on admitting this document, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could I just add, Mr. Zecevic, that in my view, at least, there would be a difference between an Official Note taken by a warden in a detention camp where one of the detainees is being interviewed by the warden on the one hand, and on the other hand an Official Note such as this one where someone like the witness is being called to give an explanation of some events that took place in the past. So, I mean, the fact that this is an Official Note does not necessarily preclude it from being tendered into evidence for its contents. I mean, I think that there's a difference between different types of Official Notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Your Honours, I do agree that there is -- that it's significantly -- there is a difference when it comes to the context when and under which circumstances the Official Note was created. I do agree with that. But as a matter -- I thought that the -- that the ruling of the Trial Chamber was a principal one, that the Official Note is created by a third person saying -- noting what somebody else said and that because of these reasons -- I mean, according to the objection -- if my recollection serves me well, according to the objection of the Office of the Prosecutor. Because if you remember, Your Honours, at that point we had even the Official Notes which were signed by the persons giving -- giving the statement. It was created by some office -- police officers and the person, at the end, signed. So I agree, there are different kinds of Official Notes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- sorry, you wanted to add something, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I did, Your Honour. I wanted to clarify something that Mr. Zecevic had said at line 30 -- page 32, line 10, because he said: "Now, this document was a part of the file. It was taken out because it's an Official Note ..." I think that's incorrect. The official file that we already put into evidence concerning this case is Exhibit P1543. It's the criminal file from the Bijeljina District Prosecution Office. And I believe the date on that document when we received it was 14 April 2005, is the date on that package. So this Official Note given by Mr. Andan on 12 December 2007 could not have been a part of that package. So it doesn't -- I think it's important for you to know that. And also, again, I think it's an important document. It's relevant to some issues, some of these contested issues. As you know, evidence is a living thing, and this changes in the course of the case. At the beginning of the case, we had certain evidence we felt made it clear that Dusko Malovic's unit was directly subordinate to Mr. Mico Stanisic. So certain were we that we put that in our chart that you have with Dusko Malovic's unit out to the side from Mr. Stanisic. Over the course of the case, there's been a series of challenges to that, and that is one reason that we felt it necessary, when we got the opportunity with the witness of some knowledge about that, to try and bolster the evidence that's already in the case through this witness. Now, absent a showing of prejudice more than you've heard so far, we think the remedy is to allow this in. Certain matters can be addressed on cross-examination. And we think that's the appropriate remedy, rather than barring the evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one clarification, Your Honours. When I said what Mr. Hannis correctly cited in the transcript, I was referring to his words on page 30, line 2: "Yes, Your Honours. This is something we received from the prosecutor's office in Bosnia. I think it's part of a file." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: For the reasons as we understand them that Mr. Hannis, in his most recent intervention, has given, we are unanimously of the view that we are surprised as to why this document was not disclosed to the Defence at an earlier stage. But notwithstanding that reservation, which, as I said, we all share, and it is such that the majority of the Bench, Judge Harhoff dissenting, Judge Harhoff's dissent being based on that various reservation which I mentioned earlier, we are satisfied that the document is such that it may be admitted having regard to the fact that the witness has adopted the contents in his testimony and we see no prejudice to the Defence which cannot be remedied in the way that Mr. Hannis has suggested, by cross-examination -- when the time comes to re-examine. And therefore the document, as I said, by a majority, is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 20141 shall be given Exhibit P2347, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. May the witness put his headphones back on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, I want to show you one more document related to the Malovic unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 20146, tab 312 of the Prosecution's list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And with the usher's help, I'd like to hand you a hard copy. Mr. Andan, just have a look at that. But while you're looking, let me ask you a question. Do you know a man named Ljubomir Borovcanin who worked in the RS Police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know him up until 1995. I think it was in 1995 that I first met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know if he was working in the Police Administration of the RS MUP in 1996?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't working there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you knew him in 1995, do you know what position he held or what section he worked in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was assistant commander of the Special Forces of the MUP of Republika Srpska. I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, just one more intervention. I think it would be important for the Trial Chamber as well. Very often, special units are mentioned. According to the regulations and laws governing the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska, there was just this one special unit. Let me not go into an explanation now, but you know, Mr. Hannis, how a person becomes a member of the Special Forces and what kind of training is required and how many years it takes. All these other special units that are being mentioned are self-styled special units. Specifically, Dusko Malovic's unit had nothing special about them except that they were big guys, as we say in Mount Romanija. So they hadn't been through any kind of training or anything. The only special unit that I acknowledge and recognise was the unit that was commanded by Mr. Karisik and later Goran Savic that was the special unit of the MUP of Republika Srpska. These others just call themselves special, and believe me they were not different from any unit in any way, except that they had a certain status within the army or the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, Mr. Malovic's unit had special status within the police; right? They were called the Special Platoon on payroll documents. Did you know that? The Special Police Platoon?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what they called them. But I tried to explain to you just now what special meant. You know how long it takes to train Special Forces. At least four years of intensive training and then three more years in a unit so that someone would be a qualified Special Forces member. In our part of the world then, someone would just put on a uniform and call himself a Special Forces guy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, I understand the thrust of your evidence, that there was nothing special about these groups, whatever they call themselves, but when you say that they had a certain status within the police, could you expand on that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, again, I'm going back to what is regulated by the law. During the war, there was just one special unit in the Ministry of the Interior and that was the unit that was commanded by Mr. Karisik and later Mr. Savic. Even that unit was not fully special, because certain members of the Ministry of the Interior were being attached to it every now and then, so they hadn't been through any kind of Special Forces training except for perhaps one platoon of that unit that had undergone such training before the war and they were, before the war, within the special unit of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were some units that called themselves special. Also, in our documents you can see that there was this special unit of Mico Davidovic's from the federal SUP. That's not correct either. These are young men who primarily provided security to individuals and facilities in the Republic of Serbia, so they were ordinary policemen. Within the federal SUP there was a brigade that provided security for public gatherings, public events, big sports matches, et cetera. And then there was also security for embassies and other buildings. Individuals who were on the move were secured by another unit. In our documents it says, for example, a special unit came from the federal SUP. It was not special in any way, believe me, except that it was the first time that I saw some weapons that they had brought in. That's what made them special in my eyes, and they were special because they had discipline and an internal establishment that did not allow for any kind of unruly or disorderly behaviour. I don't know if I've managed to paint the right picture for you, but, anyway, self-styled special units, self-styled Special Forces, were in abundance, both in the police and the military. While I was still at the Ministry of the Interior at one of our meetings, I intervened with Mr. Kljajic and I said very often every police station claims to have a special unit. I complained because a unit that was established as soon as I left Brcko was again called a special unit. It was just an intervention platoon. It was only special because it went to intervene in certain cases when public law and order were disrupted, so they did not have patrol duty, beat duty, they were there to intervene on the spot if the regular police could not get a job done. Again I'm saying the Special Police was the one that was led by Milenko Karisik and later on by Goran Savic, although later on it became something different yet again because other policemen were included in that unit who had not undergone that kind of Special Forces training. They were trained for their regular work but not for Special Forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In light of that, Mr. Andan, I think I need to show you another document before I continue with what we had on the screen at the moment. Can we show the witness Exhibit P796. This is at tab 280 of the Prosecution's list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Mr. Andan, this is a document in evidence. It's a --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is a document in evidence. It's a payroll list for the month of April 1992, and it is for the special station -- for the police station Special Platoon at the Serbian MUP, and you'll see number one is the commander Dusko Malovic and the names of some of the same people that you talked about when you identified some of the photographs. You see that? It's referred to as the special platoon at the Serbian MUP; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this document says that it's a special platoon, but I still stand by what I said: This was no special platoon. Perhaps it was treated somewhat differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand your position. You see name number 3 on this list is Zeljko Tosic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you one more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is Exhibit P984. It's at tab 276.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is another payroll, Mr. Andan. And this is for the month of October 1992. Special Platoon Sokolac. Dusko Malovic is number one on the list. I see number two is Boban Kezunovic. And number 25 is Zeljko Tosic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, could we go back to 65 ter 20146.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is the one we started to look at before, Mr. Andan, and it relates to some personnel issue concerning Zeljko Tosic. And after the cover page, take a look at the next document, which is a document from the chief of administration in the RS Public Security addressing the issue of the status of Zeljko Tosic. And in there he's indicating that the SJB, and apparently that's SJB Sokolac, does not have the required information on Tosic because he was a member of the Special Police Unit platoon strength formed in Sokolac. It goes on to say it's well known that this independent unit was first led by Dule Markovic or Malovic and then by Slobodan Kezunovic. Among other tasks, this unit provided security and escort to the minister. That was part of the task of Malovic's unit, wasn't it, to provide security for Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please specify the time, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In 1992, wasn't that part of the duties of Dusko Malovic and his unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm this. The months of June, July, and August, Mr. Malovic and his unit spent that period of time in Bijeljina, so they couldn't have been at two places at the same time. Whether something similar to this took place later, I don't know. Maybe I'm not 100 per cent correct about this, but I don't think that Mr. Stanisic remained there longer than the end of 1992. And anyway, my post was the place where I could not have been informed about the decisions of the administration. Look, is this signed by Ljubisa Borovcanin? I told you that I only met him in 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought you said 1995 originally, as the date when you met Mr. Borovcanin. Was that incorrect?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you've seen the payroll list, that there were somewhere in the neighbourhood of 25, 26, 28 members of Mr. Malovic's unit. You picked out, I think, something like eight or nine photographs from those that you were shown. Isn't it possible that a portion of Mr. Malovic's unit was not in Bijeljina with you but were with the minister wherever he was providing security? You can't account for all 26 members of the unit every day between mid-June and mid-August 1992, can you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe this calls for speculation. I understand, I must say, Mr. Hannis's frustration, but I believe the witness gave his testimony very clearly during the direct and on cross about the number of the members of the unit that were in Bijeljina. So I don't think that this is a proper question. I'm not sure that's correct. If I could have a page citation where he testified to a specific number and the fact that they were there every day between mid-June and mid-August, then I'll stand corrected. But I'm certain that was not the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I will provide you with the exact reference. But on two occasions, the witness confirmed the number of the members of the Malovic's unit that came to Bijeljina and were re-subordinated to his and Mico Davidovic's command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In any event, Mr. Hannis, any question that begins with "isn't it possible," you're starting down the road which is not likely to produce a helpful answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, then, I guess I need to rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question is: You don't know where all 26 members of Mr. Malovic's unit were every day between mid-June and mid-August 1992, do you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to make a brief introduction. It is true that I said --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, can you just answer the question and then you can explain. But that's a simple question. You don't know, do you? Because sometimes were with Mico Davidovic meeting with the army, and sometimes you were somewhere else. You don't know where every one of Malovic's unit were for every day between mid-June and mid-August, you couldn't; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can state with some certainty that they took part in all our actions in their full complement. We had mixed patrols that worked during the curfew, and it was every evening that between seven and ten of them were assigned to various areas in order to check the situation during the curfew. I cannot say that some of them did not have a sick leave or maybe a family visit, but I know that they were in all our actions and that they took part in full complement. One more thing. I answered the question and now you should allow me to say one more thing. I said that they were re-subordinated to Mr. Davidovic and myself while the actions and operations were carried out. But you have to bear in mind that their superior was Cedo Kljajic. He called Malovic to attend a meeting, as he called me and Mr. Davidovic. So he could not have been completely re-subordinated to Davidovic because he came from another country to provide assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, I'm sorry, but I don't seem to understand the last part of your answer. "He could not have been completely re-subordinated to Davidovic." Who is "he"? Do you mean Kljajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Malovic. I was referring to Mr. Malovic. I attempted to explain that they were re-subordinated to Mr. Davidovic and me. Dusko Malovic's unit was re-subordinated to Davidovic and me during the operations that were carried out in the field. But nominally, formally, their immediate superior in Bijeljina at the time was the undersecretary for public security, Mr. Cedo Kljajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As I recall your testimony on direct, you said you encountered Mr. Malovic for the first time when he came to Bijeljina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In when, June or July 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to excuse my dates again, but it was when he arrived. June or July, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you say his full component [sic] took part in every action you engaged in, how did you know what his full component was, because you only met him when I arrived in Bijeljina with however many people he arrived with? How did you know that those who came on that first date were the full component or only some lesser part of his entire unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, as far as I know, he was a non-commissioned officer in the JNA. The rules and regulations that he had learned in the army, he applied in the unit as well. Every time an operation was carried out, his subordinate would report to him and inform him whether any of the members were sick or absent. So as I stated during examination-in-chief, as you call it, they were a strengthened platoon, 20 to 25 people. Maybe I even stated once or twice 30 people. I did not count them. That is true. However, when we are all lined up, then we have first the report on the manpower, then we have the report on any possible problems, and that's exactly the same procedure followed by Mr. Malovic's unit. So don't ask me to specify whether there were 19 or 23 of them. But what I heard when they were about to carry out an operation was that nobody was absent and that they were ready to carry out the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you have a look at the document in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
